paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism (AR-JP) is a levodopa-responsive parkinsonism. Pathologically it shows highly selective degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the zona compacta of the substantia nigra (Matsumine et al., 1997). Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996) described it as a distinct clinical entity with early onset and slow progression. In their patients the parkinsonian triad was mild, while gait freezing, hyperreflexia, foot dystonia, and retropulsion were relatively prominent, and symptoms improved after sleep. Levodopa-induced dyskinesia and wearing-off phenomenon were frequent.

paragraphs.text: Takahashi et al. (1994) described a family in which 4 of 5 sibs developed a similar juvenile-onset parkinsonism that improved after sleep. The parents were first cousins. One sib, a 67-year-old woman, came to autopsy. Pathologic changes were confined to the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNPC) and the locus ceruleus. The SNPC showed obvious neuronal loss and gliosis in the medial and ventrolateral regions. In the rest of the SNPC and in the locus ceruleus, neurons were reduced in number and most had low melanin content, but there was no detectable gliosis. There were no Lewy bodies, and the overall picture differed from Lewy body Parkinson disease.

The authors also found neuronal loss and fibrillary gliosis in the substantia nigra pars reticulata, which had not been reported previously in AR-JP.

paragraphs.text: Kay et al. (2010) tested 1,686 controls and 2,091 patients with Parkinson disease for PARK2 deletions, multiplications, and copy number variants (CNVs). Heterozygous CNVs were found in 0.95% of controls and 0.86% of patients. CNVs in the 16 control carriers were all in exons 1-4, sparing exons that encode functionally critical domains, whereas mutations in patients spanned exons 2-9. Thirteen patients had 2 CNVs, 5 had 1 CNV and 1 point mutation, and 18 had 1 CNV. In whites, a single CNV was not associated with increased risk of Parkinson disease (odds ratio 1.05) or with earlier onset.

paragraphs.text: Zhu et al. (2022) evaluated PRKN mutations in the NIH-PD + AMP-PD case-control cohort (whole genome sequencing in 4,094 participants) and in the UK Biobank. In UK Biobank genotyping array data from nearly half a million participants, they identified 2,692 PRKN CNVs. About half involved exon 2, and 88% involved exons 2, 3, or 4. In the UK Biobank, 1.8% of participants carried 1 pathogenic PRKN mutation. Carriers were as likely as noncarriers to have Parkinson disease (odds ratio 0.91) or a parent with Parkinson disease. Results in the NIH-PD + AMP-PD cohort were similar (odds ratio 1.29). Functional assays in patient fibroblasts resolved variants of unclear significance in biallelic carriers.

paragraphs.text: Lohmann et al. (2003) compared 146 early-onset parkinsonism patients with parkin mutations and 250 without. No single sign distinguished the groups. Patients with mutations had earlier and more symmetrical onset, dystonia at onset and hyperreflexia more often, slower progression, and a tendency toward greater levodopa response at lower doses. On multivariate analysis, dystonia at onset and brisk reflexes correlated with age at onset rather than with mutation status. The younger the onset, the slower the progression. Carriers of at least 1 missense mutation had higher UPDRS motor scores than carriers of 2 truncating mutations. Missense mutations in functional domains led to earlier onset. Patients with a single heterozygous mutation had later and more asymmetrical onset and more levodopa-induced fluctuations and dystonia than patients with 2 mutations.

paragraphs.text: Mortiboys et al. (2008) studied fibroblasts from 5 patients with homozygous or compound heterozygous parkin mutations. Mitochondrial membrane potential was lower in all 5 by an average of 30%, and complex I activity was lower by an average of 42%. Complex I-linked ATP production was reduced, and cellular ATP levels were reduced by 58%. Mitochondrial branching was increased and correlated with reduced complex I-linked ATP production. FRAP assays showed reduced functional connectivity of the mitochondrial matrix, which worsened after rotenone exposure. siRNA knockdown of parkin in control fibroblasts reproduced these defects, whereas 50% knockdown, mimicking haploinsufficiency, did not. The glutathione precursor OTCA restored membrane potential to 95% of control levels, apparently through a compensatory increase in complex II activity.

paragraphs.text: Hedrich et al. (2001) showed that mutation analysis of the parkin gene should include gene dosage studies, because dosage alterations were missed by conventional screening. Lücking et al. (2001) likewise recommended sensitive techniques such as semiquantitative multiplex PCR and said pseudodominant inheritance must be considered in early-onset parkinsonism. Ohsawa et al. (2005) suggested that reduced sural SNAP amplitude could be a diagnostic indicator of PARK2. Kay et al. (2007) cautioned that a single heterozygous point mutation should not be taken as the cause of disease unless supported by family data and functional studies.

agent.process_note: I opened all 39 files. Three had full text, which I read in full: Mortiboys 2008, Marder 2010 and Alcalay 2010. The other 36 were abstracts only, except Yamamura 1973 and Bonifati 1994, which had titles only. I left Bonifati 1994 uncited because its title, about anticipation in familial PD, has no clear tie to this entry. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so the intro gives no gene MIM number; the 6q25.2-q27 location comes from the papers. Hoenicka 2002 writes '225delA' while Marder 2010 and Mortiboys 2008 write '255delA'. I kept each as written and did not merge them. For many abstract-only variants (V56E, C212Y, Klein's deletions) the specific zygosity or exon details were not in the abstract, so I left those gaps.
